strengths: Timely and important contribution: First comprehensive safety analysis of dLLMs with novel vulnerability decomposition (intra-step vs inter-step), particularly the Denoising-path Dependence finding which provides genuine new insights into dLLM generation mechanics

Well-motivated and elegant defense design: Stochastic Annealing Remasking with step-aware decay (Eq. 8) elegantly addresses safety-quality tradeoff by concentrating randomness early; Block-level Audit and Repair grounded in representation-based safety research

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 dLLM models, multiple attack paradigms (6 methods), diverse datasets, general capability preservation (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval), latency analysis, ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies

Strong empirical results: 33.2% relative ASR reduction (47.9%→14.7%) across diverse attacks with negligible performance degradation and inference overhead; consistent improvements across different models
Practical and deployable: Training-free framework functions as plug-and-play module, improving real-world adoption prospects
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters (Tables 3-6), algorithm specification (Appendix D), comprehensive experimental setup documentation, and code availability promised
weaknesses: Limited dLLM-specific attack evaluation: Only 2 true dLLM-specific attacks tested (PAD, DIJA); most attacks adapted from AR LLM literature (GCG, AutoDAN). Unclear if evaluated attacks represent optimal dLLM-specific threats. Critical for a safety paper at top venue.

Safety Divergence metric lacks rigorous validation: Eq. 9 uses heuristic cosine distance of mean hidden states at output layer, step 1 without sufficient justification. Missing: ablation on metric choice/layer/step; validation against alternatives; analysis of adaptive attacks circumventing detection via knowledge of threshold

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines portability: α₀ varies 0.3-0.7 across models (Table 6); no principled selection strategy for new models. Contradicts 'plug-and-play' claim. Sensitivity analysis (Table 7-8) shows non-trivial performance gaps (≤8% ASR variation)

Block-level Repair applied only to first block: Defense ignores harmful content emerging in later blocks. Justification based on efficiency insufficient for safety-critical application. Missing analysis of attack fraction exploiting later blocks

No evaluation against adaptive attacks: Threat model assumes attackers unaware of DIFFUGUARD. No white-box adversarial evaluation where attackers know defense mechanisms and hyperparameters. Safety of heuristic metrics unvalidated

Weak baseline comparisons: Only 2 baselines (PPL-Filter, Self-reminder). Self-reminder produces dramatic improvements (93.65%→30.58% on LLaDA PAD), suggesting orthogonal defenses confound DIFFUGUARD contribution. Missing comparisons to guided decoding, representation-based methods

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported. Some 0.00% baseline ASR values (e.g., GCG on Dream) appear suspiciously low. No inter-rater agreement for LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation; no manual validation

Limited theoretical understanding: Step-aware decay (Eq. 8) motivated empirically without principled justification. Why does early randomness work? Why is mean hidden state divergence optimal? Lack theoretical grounding
Generalization concerns: Only 4 models, all 7B-8B scale. No evaluation on larger models, different architectures, or non-mask-diffusion variants. Limited to single prompt examples
Incomplete failure analysis: Table 1 shows varying defense effectiveness but limited discussion. No adversarial examples or case studies of failure modes. Figure 8 shows successes only

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem in emerging dLLM safety research with clear practical relevance
Provides comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 models, 6 attack methods, and multiple datasets with ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Clear structural decomposition into intra-step and inter-step vulnerabilities, with well-designed controlled experiments validating key phenomena (Denoising-path Dependence)
Practical training-free plug-and-play approach with substantial empirical improvements (ASR: 47.9% → 14.7%) and minimal latency overhead
Maintains general model capabilities while improving safety, demonstrated across MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Stochastic Annealing Remasking is straightforward noise injection with decay; Block-level Audit and Repair uses standard cosine-distance anomaly detection and logit suppression—no genuinely novel mechanisms introduced

Safety Divergence metric is underspecified and problematic: prompt decomposition into p_origin/p_template lacks systematic procedure; mean-pooled representation distance is theoretically unjustified; assumes white-box access and attack structure knowledge

Weak baselines: Only PPL-Filter and Self-reminder compared; missing comparisons with safety-aligned training (DPO, RLHF) or stronger defense mechanisms; threat model ambiguity between claimed white-box setting and attacks tested

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Denoising-path Dependence is empirically observed but not explained; Safety-Quality tradeoff is generic, not specific to dLLMs; greedy remasking harm shown empirically but not principled

Methodological concerns: Only 7B-8B models tested; hyperparameters vary significantly across models suggesting per-model tuning; GCG achieves 0% ASR on vanilla models raising dataset validity questions; no inter-rater reliability for ASR evaluation

Robustness issues: Probability suppression (Eq. 10) easily circumvented using synonyms; no evaluation against adaptive attacks; Block-level Repair only applied to first block (arbitrary limitation); no failure mode analysis

Generalization concerns: Results on small open-source models; unclear scaling to larger models; decomposition procedure for complex jailbreaks (DIJA, WildJailbreak) not formally defined; limited explanation of why findings should transfer

Presentation and reproducibility: Dense notation; Algorithm 1 in appendix; no code provided at review time; missing implementation details (k selection, exact p_origin extraction procedure); unclear mathematical justification for Eq. 7 (mixing uniform [0,1] with logits)

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: First systematic analysis of dLLM jailbreak vulnerabilities, an emerging area requiring safety research
Well-structured analysis framework: Clear decomposition into intra-step and inter-step dimensions provides intuitive organization and actionable insights
Novel empirical observations: Denoising-path Dependence is well-demonstrated with strong quantitative evidence (e.g., 22.6% ASR difference between early vs. mid-stage intervention)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 models, 6 attack methods, 3 safety datasets, plus 3 capability benchmarks; proper ablation studies validating design choices
Practical deployable solution: Training-free framework with minimal latency overhead (<5%) and negligible performance degradation on general capabilities
Strong empirical results: Consistent ASR reductions across diverse attacks (47.9%→14.7% average; 96.8%→27.9% against PAD/DIJA specifically designed for dLLMs)
Reproducibility: Algorithm formally specified, detailed hyperparameters provided in appendices, code availability promised
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in defense components: Stochastic Annealing Remasking is essentially interpolating confidence-based and random selection with a decay schedule; Block-level Audit and Repair uses standard representation distance and token suppression. While effective, these are incremental applications of established techniques

Safety Divergence metric lacks justification: (1) Why cosine distance specifically? Alternatives not discussed. (2) Assumes clean decomposition of p₀ into p_origin⊕p_template, which may not generalize beyond in-place prompting attacks. (3) Threshold λ shows sensitivity (Table 8) with limited guidance for practitioners. (4) Only repairs first block, raising concerns about later harmful content

Incomplete threat model: (1) Assumes white-box access (logits); black-box scenarios underexplored. (2) Only 2 of 6 attacks are dLLM-specific (PAD, DIJA); most transferred from AR LLMs. (3) GCG trained on LLaMA-3-8B then transferred to dLLMs—true exploitation of dLLM vulnerabilities unclear. (4) Acknowledges future adaptive attacks may find new vulnerabilities

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: Requires model-specific tuning (α₀=0.3 for LLaDA, α₀=0.7 for Dream). No methodology for selecting hyperparameters for new models. Trade-off between safety and quality evident but guidance limited

Analysis lacks depth on fundamental causes: While parallel generation and iterative refinement naturally create different vulnerabilities, limited exploration of *why* dLLMs are fundamentally more vulnerable beyond architectural observations. Theoretical understanding could be deeper

Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares to PPL-Filter and Self-reminder (both simple baselines). No comparison to other representation-based safety detection methods or defenses specifically designed for diffusion models

Incomplete failure mode analysis: Case studies show only successful defenses (Figure 8). No systematic analysis of attack types DIFFUGUARD fails against. MMaDA shows dramatically worse performance even with defense (40.4% avg ASR, Table 1)—underlying causes not thoroughly investigated

Model-specific analysis incomplete: Section 3 primarily analyzes LLaDA-8B; different model families (Dream, LLaDA, MMaDA) show vastly different vulnerability profiles (1.05-2.35% vs 14.25-61.55% on WildJailbreak) but underlying reasons not explored. E.1 mentions 'Safety Tax' but lacks depth

Evaluation reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge: No human evaluation validating GPT-4o-mini reliability. Binary SAFE/UNSAFE classification doesn't capture partial compliance severity. PPL may not capture semantic quality degradation

strengths: Timely contribution addressing safety vulnerabilities in emerging dLLM paradigm with clear problem formulation
Novel vulnerability characterization through intra-step/inter-step decomposition and identification of Denoising-path Dependence phenomenon
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 models, 6 attack methods, and multiple evaluation approaches with strong empirical results (47.9% → 14.7% ASR)
Practical training-free framework with negligible latency overhead and minimal impact on model utility
Well-structured presentation with thorough reproducibility details, ablation studies, and adaptive attack evaluation
weaknesses: Defense mechanisms lack novelty: stochastic annealing is standard noise injection with linear schedule (no justification), block-level audit builds incrementally on existing hidden state detection with ad-hoc probability suppression (Eq. 10)

Critical practical limitation: prompt decomposition into p_origin ⊕ p_template is never rigorously defined and unlikely generalizes beyond known attack templates; severely limits applicability to novel attack paradigms

Hyperparameter selection unprincipled: λ (safety threshold), γ (remask ratio), and M (extra steps) require manual tuning with high sensitivity (Table 8); no method for setting thresholds for new threat types
White-box access requirement fundamentally restricts real-world deployment to scenarios with full model access; not applicable to API-only systems
Adaptive attacks expose vulnerability: gradient-based and threshold-probing attacks maintain 35-84% success rates (Table 9), suggesting fundamental fragility; insufficient analysis of why
Evaluation concerns: baseline GCG ASR of 0% on AdvBench appears unrealistic; high reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge primary metric despite known limitations; human evaluation limited to 200 samples
Narrow threat model: inference-time only, excludes training-time attacks; artificial experimental setup (Section 3.3 token injection) with unclear transfer to realistic scenarios
Missing analysis: no failure case discussion, limited baseline comparisons (only weak baselines), incomplete justification for technical choices (cosine distance, −∞ logits, linear annealing)

strengths: Addresses timely and important safety problem in emerging dLLM models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 models, 6 attacks, and multiple metrics
Practical training-free defense with minimal latency/utility impact
Strong empirical results with thorough ablations and hyperparameter analysis
Clear problem decomposition into intra-step and inter-step vulnerabilities
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: SAR combines standard techniques (randomization + annealing); Safety Divergence heavily builds on prior work (Zhou et al., Arditi et al.)
Denoising-path Dependence claim overstated: artificial token injection experiments; similar phenomena known in AR LLMs (Qi et al., 2024); distinction argued via bidirectional attention not convincing
Significant adaptive attack vulnerability: simple gradient-based and threshold-probing attacks achieve 35-65% ASR (Table 9)

Critical methodological gaps: prompt decomposition (p_origin extraction) lacks practical detail; λ threshold highly sensitive (Table 8) without principled setting; per-model hyperparameter tuning (α₀=0.3 vs 0.7) questions generalization
Limited dLLM-specific attacks: only PAD and DIJA are native; GCG/AutoDAN adapted from AR LLMs
First-block-only repair is significant limitation not adequately justified or analyzed
No comparison with cited dLLM-specific defenses (Zhang et al. 2025b, Wen et al. 2025); unclear how approach scales to new attacks
Implementation issues: Eq. 10 (setting logits to -∞) crude; Algorithm 1 missing key details (top-k′ determination); unclear how model avoids regenerating semantically similar harmful content
Evaluation concerns: LLM-as-Judge primary metric with limited human evaluation (200 samples); ASR metric limitations not discussed
Core findings questionable: forced token injection unrealistic; connection between inter-step analysis and why BLAAR works unclear

strengths: First comprehensive safety analysis of dLLMs with novel vulnerability findings (Denoising-path Dependence) specific to parallel and iterative generation mechanisms
Well-decomposed analysis into intra-step and inter-step vulnerabilities with strong empirical validation through controlled experiments (Figures 4-5)
Comprehensive evaluation across 4 dLLM variants, 6 jailbreak methods, and multiple assessment approaches with detailed ablations and adaptive attack scenarios
Practical training-free solution deployable as plug-and-play module with negligible latency overhead while preserving model utility
Thorough documentation with detailed hyperparameter settings, extensive appendices, code availability, and clear algorithmic specification
weaknesses: Defense mechanisms are incremental: Stochastic Annealing Remasking is straightforward confidence-score perturbation, and Safety Divergence heavily borrows from existing work without substantial innovation
Hyperparameter selection lacks transparency; different α₀ values across models without clear methodology, and no guidance for new architectures; no discussion of test-set tuning
Significant performance variance across dLLM families (e.g., Dream 2.35% vs MMaDA 14.25% ASR on WildJailbreak) suggests model-specific tuning may be necessary, limiting generalization
Safety Divergence decomposition into p_origin and p_template is not clearly defined for complex prompts and appears tailored to in-place prompting attacks; applicability to other attacks unclear
Block-level Audit only applies to first block due to latency constraints; limited analysis of potential vulnerabilities in later blocks and when this limitation is critical
Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple random seeds; single-run results; limited baseline comparisons (only 2 simple baselines)
All experiments on 7-8B models; unclear scalability to larger models and unclear how method generalizes to future dLLM architectures with different generation paradigms
Table 1 shows non-negligible residual ASR in some scenarios (e.g., GCGAdvBench on MMaDA: 0.45%); limited discussion of attack types where defense is less effective
